title: Jackfruit in Beer: Taming a Loud Fruit | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew with ripe jackfruit: handling the sticky latex, dosing a very loud aroma and the wheat beers and pale ales it suits.
teaser: Jackfruit is the loudest fruit in the market. In beer, the trick is using less than you think.
standfirst: Ripe jackfruit smells of banana, pineapple and bubblegum all at once. That makes it a natural partner for wheat beer yeast and a risky one for anything delicate. Here is how we prepare it and how much to use.
sections: Jackfruit aroma is strong enough to take over

Ripe jackfruit bulbs (the fleshy pods around each seed) are sweet and intensely fragrant. The smell sits somewhere between banana, pineapple and mango, with a heavy, almost fermented edge when the fruit is very ripe. Overripe jackfruit can tip into onion and rot, which no beer will hide.

The sugar is high for a fruit, often well above 15 °Brix in fully ripe bulbs. So jackfruit adds real fermentable sugar as well as aroma. Account for it: a few points of extra gravity and a little more alcohol than the base beer would give alone.
Handle the latex before anything else

Cut a jackfruit and a white, sticky latex runs from the rind and core. It glues itself to knives, hands and fermenter walls. Rub cooking oil on your hands and blade first, as every South Indian kitchen does. Work on newspaper you can throw away.

Use only the bulbs. Remove every seed and the stringy rags between bulbs. The seeds are good roasted or in a curry, but not in the fermenter. Weigh the cleaned bulbs: they are often only a third of the whole fruit by weight.
Dose low and taste your way up

Jackfruit is not a fruit to use at 250 grams per litre. Start at 50 to 100 grams of cleaned bulbs per litre of beer. A 20 litre batch at 75 g/L needs 1.5 kg of bulbs, about what a small fruit gives.

Freeze the bulbs first. Freezing ruptures cells, releases juice and reduces wild microbes. Thaw, chop or blend roughly, then add after primary fermentation has slowed. A fine purée extracts faster but makes racking harder, so a coarse chop in a mesh bag is a good compromise.

Taste after three days. Jackfruit extracts quickly. The aroma tends to peak within a week. Leaving it longer adds pulpy, vegetal notes rather than more fruit.
Why wheat beer yeast and jackfruit get on

A German hefeweizen yeast fermented at 18 to 20 °C makes isoamyl acetate, the banana ester. Jackfruit carries a similar banana note. Put them together and the fruit seems to belong to the beer, rather than sitting on top of it.

The catch is that the two can pile up into bubblegum. Ferment the wheat beer at the cooler end of the yeast's range so it leans to clove rather than banana, then let the jackfruit bring the fruit. This is the one floor detail we would insist on: 18 °C, not 22 °C, when the fruit is going in later.

Other good bases are a pale ale with a modest dose of tropical hops, a Belgian blonde, or a light lager where the fruit is the only flavour on show.
Count the sugar the bulbs bring

Jackfruit is sweet enough that it changes the beer's strength, so measure it. Blend a few bulbs, squeeze the pulp through a cloth and put a drop of juice on a refractometer. Ripe bulbs often read around 20 °Brix.

At 75 grams of bulbs per litre and 20 °Brix, the fruit adds about 15 grams of sugar per litre. That is roughly 6 gravity points, or close to 0.8% extra ABV once the yeast has eaten it. A wheat beer brewed to 5% will finish nearer 5.7%. That matters for your label, for the beer's balance and for anyone counting drinks.

The sugar also feeds a brief second fermentation. Leave room in the fermenter, keep the airlock or spunding valve working and do not bottle until the gravity has held steady for three days. A sealed bottle of half-fermented fruit beer is a hazard, not a treat.

Jackfruit season runs through the hot months, broadly March to July, in Kerala, coastal Karnataka, the Konkan and parts of the north east. That is also the worst time of year for fermentation control in most Indian homes. Plan ahead: freeze cleaned bulbs in season, then brew the beer when nights are cooler.

Frozen bulbs sealed in bags keep well for months. Label them with the date and weight so you know exactly what you are adding. Our guide to adding fruit to beer covers sanitising and racking in more detail.

• Too much fruit. The beer smells like the fruit stall at closing time.
  • Overripe fruit. Sulphury, oniony notes come through and never fade.
  • Latex in the fermenter. A sticky film that traps yeast and is miserable to clean.
  • High bitterness. Jackfruit sweetness and sharp hop bitterness taste disjointed. Keep IBU under 25.

Most of these are judgement calls about balance: how much fruit a base beer can carry and which yeast character will support it. That judgement is what a style course trains. It is hard to pick up from a single recipe.

Your first step: buy half a ripe jackfruit, clean and freeze the bulbs, then dose a litre of finished wheat beer at 75 g/L and taste it daily for a week.
faqs: How do I stop jackfruit latex sticking to everything?
Oil your hands and knife before cutting, work on disposable paper and use only the cleaned bulbs. Keep rind, core and rags out of the beer.
How much jackfruit should I use in beer?
Start at 50 to 100 grams of cleaned bulbs per litre. Jackfruit aroma is very strong, so it is easier to add more later than to fix an overloaded beer.
What beer style suits jackfruit best?
A German style wheat beer fermented cool works well, because its banana and clove notes support the fruit. A light pale ale or Belgian blonde also suits it.
